<!-- head-1: body_md -->
{\it If the function $f:\mathbb{R}_+ \to \mathbb{R}_+$ is absolutely integrable, then for any $p\geq 0$ the Laplace transform
\begin{equation} 
\bigl( \mathscr{L} f\bigr) (p) = \overline{f}(p) = \int_0^{\infty} \!{\rm d} t\: e^{-p t} f(t)
\end{equation}
is a non-increasing function of $p$.}
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
Let $p'>p>0$. Then $\overline{f}(p') = \int_0^{\infty} \!{\rm d} t\: e^{-p' t} f(t) \leq \int_0^{\infty} \!{\rm d} t\: e^{-p t} f(t) = \overline{f}(p)$. \hfill q.e.d. \\

For $x>0$, the Laplace-transformed equation (\ref{eq:B1}) becomes $p \overline{u}(p,x) -T = D \partial_x^2\overline{u}(p,x)$. Since a special solution is $\overline{u}_{\rm sp}=\frac{T}{p}$, the general solution of this is
\begin{equation} 
\overline{u}(p,x) = u_{+} e^{+\sqrt{p/D\,}\, x} + u_{-} e^{-\sqrt{p/D\,}\, x} + \frac{T}{p}
\end{equation} 
with free constants $u_{\pm}$. 
Herein, the first term is an increasing function of $p$ and cannot be interpreted as a Laplace-transform. We discard it by setting $u_+=0$. The boundary condition $u(t,0)=1$ leads to $\overline{u}(p,0)=1/p$, hence
$u_{-}=(1-T)/p$ and
\begin{equation}
\overline{u}(p,x) = \frac{1-T}{p} e^{-\sqrt{p/D\,}\, x} + \frac{T}{p}
\end{equation}
The inverse Laplace-transform of this, using \cite[(2.2.1.16)]{Prudnikov5}, leads back to (\ref{gl:final}).
<!-- end head-2 -->
